label: Legacy Letter
summary: A letter passing on your values, lessons, and blessing to someone who matters, while you can still say it yourself.

slots.label: Values
slots.description: What the author actually organized their life around, pulled from real decisions in the context pack — a value without an episode is a poster, not a legacy.

slots.label: Lessons
slots.description: What life taught them, told through where it was learned; the hard-won lessons matter most, including what the lesson cost.

slots.label: Gratitude
slots.description: What this specific recipient gave the author, named through real moments — the movement recipients reread most.

slots.label: Forgiveness
slots.description: The rarest movement, in both directions where true: what the author asks forgiveness for, and what they extend it for. Only what the material supports — never fabricated contrition.

slots.label: Hopes and Blessings
slots.description: What the author wishes for this person, said plainly as blessing, not instruction — the closing movement that leaves the recipient held.

research.basis: The ethical-will/tzava'ah tradition (roughly 3,500 years old) and Barry Baines' modern revival of it rest on the same claim Lifehug's context pack already satisfies: legacy lands when it's tied to real decisions and named moments, not abstract advice. Baines' framework treats forgiveness and forward-looking blessing as distinct movements, which is why they're sequenced rather than merged. The template's own closing rule — end on the blessing, not the forgiveness — is honored by placing hopes_and_blessings last among the five slots.
citations: Baines, Ethical Wills: Putting Your Values on Paper — the modern authority reviving the tzava'ah tradition for lay use; values and lessons must be anchored to real decisions and cost, not stated as maxims.
Tzava'ah tradition (~3,500 years, Jewish ethical wills) — passing values, wisdom, and blessing to descendants while the elder can still say it themselves, distinct from a legal or financial will.

Seligman et al. 2005; Klass, Silverman & Nickman 1996 (adjacent) — naming specific recipient-given moments (gratitude movement) over general praise carries more weight, consistent with the specificity effect found in gratitude-letter and continuing-bonds writing.

ai_context: Draft in this slot order — values, lessons, gratitude, forgiveness, hopes_and_blessings — so the letter ends on the blessing regardless of how the five movements are numbered elsewhere; the template's closing instruction (end on the blessing, not the forgiveness) takes precedence over the movement list's own numbering.
